question: Does the FAERS abaloparatide urate/gout lead survive controlled safety review, and is there a source-grounded PTH1R-to-ABCG2 mechanism worth testing without claiming that the mechanism is established?

load_bearing_verifications.claim: In the postmenopausal osteoporosis trial, 25% of abaloparatide recipients versus 6% of placebo recipients with normal baseline urate had at least one post-baseline value above the normal range; the label did not associate this laboratory finding with increased gout or arthralgia.

The FDA clinical review reports mean serum-urate changes at months 1, 6, and 18 of +46.1, +62.2, and +44.5 micromol/L for abaloparatide versus -0.1, -2.7, and -1.7 micromol/L for placebo; one participant in each arm developed gout.
load_bearing_verifications.primary_source: FDA NDA 208743 clinical review, Table 68 and hyperuricemia safety discussion

load_bearing_verifications.claim: The Japanese controlled study reported a week-78 mean urate change of +0.98 mg/dL on abaloparatide versus -0.06 mg/dL on placebo, with abnormal variation in 27.1% versus 1.4%.
load_bearing_verifications.primary_source: PMDA Ostabalo review report, uric-acid safety tables

load_bearing_verifications.claim: The smaller male osteoporosis trial showed 7% on abaloparatide versus 6% on placebo crossing above the normal urate range and did not demonstrate increased gout or arthralgia.

PTH(1-34) reduced plasma-membrane ABCG2 in Caco-2 cells without reducing ABCG2 mRNA or total protein; in uremic rats, renal and intestinal membrane ABCG2 and urate excretion fell, and cinacalcet prevented the changes.
ACTIVExtend cannot test continued abaloparatide exposure because all continuing participants switched to alendronate.
Abaloparatide raises serum urate by causing PTH1R-dependent loss of renal or intestinal surface ABCG2.
load_bearing_verifications.primary_source: No study directly measured abaloparatide, ABCG2 trafficking, and urate flux together.
load_bearing_verifications.status: unverified — retained only as a Research Conjecture with a discriminating experiment

limitations: The controlled trials establish a serum-urate effect, not an increased incidence of gout.
The male trial was smaller and did not reproduce a clear urate-range separation; no sex interaction is established.
Sugimoto et al. tested PTH(1-34) in Caco-2 cells, uremic rats, and a secondary-hyperparathyroidism context, not abaloparatide in healthy human intestine or proximal tubule.
ACTIVExtend switched all participants to alendronate and therefore is not a continued-exposure test.
Regional native-language searches were bounded and did not contribute a load-bearing non-English claim; no absence claim was drawn from them.
No non-English load-bearing text was used, so the two-model translation protocol was not triggered.
errors: The initial sandboxed PubMed snapshot attempt failed on DNS; the same generated plan succeeded when rerun through the approved network path.
ClinicalTrials.gov API retrieval returned internal errors; the trial registry pages, primary publications, and regulatory reviews were used instead.
Several native-language PubMed queries returned the same English osteoporosis records regardless of the native term and were not used as regional evidence.
